rewrites.title: Time course of chromatin marks at primed enhancers after factor withdrawal
rewrites.description: Run a CUT&RUN/CUT&Tag time course for AP-1 occupancy, H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and nucleosome positioning at primed enhancers after factor withdrawal. Add DNA-FISH/Hi-C for enhancer repositioning and mitotic-chromosome staining for AP-1 bookmarking in synchronized cells. This separates heritable chromatin marks that outlive the factor from re-recruitment of AP-1 each cycle.

rewrites.title: Sufficiency test by targeted AP-1 recruitment with histone and DNA-methylation readouts
rewrites.description: Recruit JUN or FOS to a synthetic reporter or a chosen enhancer with dCas9 or a Gal4 system for a limited time, then release it and watch the reporter over many cell divisions. Pair this with ChIP or CUT&Tag for H3K27ac and H3K4me1 and with methylation profiling, and test cooperation with the SWI/SNF (BAF) complex using a BRG1 inhibitor. Persistent activity and marks after release would show that AP-1 alone is sufficient to set a memory state. A lack of persistence would show that it is not.

rewrites.title: Single-cell transient AP-1 perturbation in otherwise identical cells
rewrites.description: In a clonal, unstimulated population, use dCas9-based activation or optogenetic FOS/JUN dimerization to transiently drive AP-1 only in sparse, trackable cells. Follow those cells and their progeny by live imaging and matched single-cell multiome. If a brief, cell-autonomous AP-1 pulse alone shifts long-term state and drug response relative to neighbors in the same dish, AP-1 is causally sufficient for memory rather than a correlate of upstream signaling.

rewrites.title: Second-hit amplification as the functional readout
rewrites.description: Prime cells, wait, then re-challenge and quantify gains in response rate, amplitude, and the fraction of responding cells at candidate AP-1 memory loci. Show specificity by deleting the TRE motif or CRISPRi-silencing the individual primed enhancer, so that amplification is lost locus-specifically rather than only upon global AP-1 depletion.

rewrites.title: Stimulus-withdrawal ATAC/CUT&Tag time course
rewrites.description: Stimulate cells (e.g., with TPA, injury, or inflammatory signal), then remove the stimulus and track AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding, chromatin accessibility, and H3K27ac at AP-1 motif sites over days to weeks. Persistent accessibility after AP-1 levels return to baseline would mark sites with memory. The question is whether the sites stay accessible and marked after the driving signal stops.

rewrites.title: Acute AP-1 degradation to separate initiation from maintenance
rewrites.description: Use a degron (dTAG/AID) on FOS or JUN, or a dominant-negative such as A-FOS, and remove AP-1 at different times after the stimulus: before, during, and long after. If accessibility and the faster re-induction of target genes persist after AP-1 is gone, AP-1 is needed only to establish the memory. If they collapse, AP-1 is needed to maintain it.

rewrites.title: Single-cell lineage tracing of AP-1 states across divisions
rewrites.description: Use live-cell AP-1 activity reporters (e.g., endogenously tagged FOS/JUN or a TRE-driven fluorescent reporter) with time-lapse imaging of mother-daughter pairs to measure whether AP-1 activity state is inherited and correlated between sister cells beyond what shared stimulus explains. Quantify autocorrelation across generations to distinguish heritable bistable states from re-induced noise.

rewrites.title: Single-cell AP-1 history predicts future response
rewrites.description: Use a live knock-in fluorescent reporter of AP-1 activity to track individual cells through repeated stimuli, recording each cell's prior AP-1 pulse history. Test whether that history predicts the magnitude and speed of the cell's response to a later stimulus, and whether AP-1 inhibitors such as T-5224 erase this predictive relationship. A history-dependent response that disappears with AP-1 inhibition directly links AP-1 activity to cellular memory.

rewrites.title: Lineage-resolved memory with a live AP-1 reporter
rewrites.description: Test whether the memory is heritable using a fluorescent AP-1-responsive reporter or a FosTRAP-style lineage recorder, following single cells through several divisions by time-lapse microscopy. Measure whether daughter cells inherit the primed state and whether the fraction that retains it decays on a predictable schedule, as expected for a memory rather than a transient response.

rewrites.title: Dose-and-duration single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics
rewrites.description: Use live reporters (FOS-GFP, AP-1 transcriptional reporters, JUN-N-terminal-kinase sensors) in single cells. Give pulsed or escalating inputs. Test whether the history of AP-1 activity, such as its dynamics, cumulative integral and frequency, predicts later gene expression and cell fate better than current AP-1 levels do. Analyze with information-theoretic and hysteresis measures, and look for inheritance of states in daughter cells after division.

rewrites.title: Per-site decay constants of AP-1 sites after transient stimulus
rewrites.description: Run a dense time course (hours to weeks) after a transient stimulus measuring FOS/JUN occupancy (CUT&RUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC), and AP-1 protein levels, fitting a per-site decay constant to classify elements as transient versus long-lived. Memory predicts a reproducible subpopulation whose accessibility half-life far exceeds that of AP-1 occupancy. Single-molecule tracking of Halo-JUN would test whether persistence reflects longer residence time rather than more protein.

rewrites.title: Single-cell and lineage-tracked heritability of AP-1 states
rewrites.description: Use live-cell reporters of AP-1 activity (e.g., a FOS promoter reporter or a JUN kinase translocation reporter) combined with lineage tracking or barcoding, plus single-cell multiome (scRNA and scATAC) data. Measure whether AP-1 state or enhancer accessibility is inherited by daughter cells more than expected by chance, and whether it is bimodal or hysteretic, as expected for a self-sustaining feedback loop.

rewrites.title: Lineage barcoding plus AP-1 reporter across cell divisions
rewrites.description: Combine heritable lineage barcodes (e.g., Watermelon/CellTag-style) with a live AP-1 transcriptional reporter and single-cell RNA/ATAC readout, so that an individual cell's AP-1 state before a perturbation can be linked to the behavior of its descendants many divisions later. Memory predicts intra-clone concordance of AP-1 activity and downstream fate that exceeds what is expected from shared transient signaling, and that concordance should decay with a measurable half-life in generations.

rewrites.title: Inducible degradation of AP-1 during the memory window
rewrites.description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-based degron on endogenous FOS or JUN to remove AP-1 after priming but before re-stimulation. If AP-1 is the memory carrier, degradation should erase the re-induction advantage while leaving the first-response induction intact. Timing the degradation separately from the priming stimulus separates maintenance of memory from its initial establishment.

rewrites.title: Pulse-release kinetics of FOS/JUN
rewrites.description: Place FOS/JUN under optogenetic or dTAG/auxin degron control, deliver a defined pulse, then fully remove the factor and measure the decay half-life of the downstream state (ATAC accessibility, target RNA, drug-resistant colony formation) relative to division time. Persistence across many divisions after the input is gone is the operational signature of memory; rapid relaxation marks it as a maintained steady state.

rewrites.title: Re-stimulation challenge: primed vs. naive transcriptional response
rewrites.description: Give two pulses of stimulus separated by variable rest intervals and measure nascent RNA (PRO-seq or scRNA-seq) of AP-1 target genes after the second pulse. Memory predicts faster or stronger induction in primed cells, with a decay time that can be fitted to a model. Test whether this priming requires AP-1 by degrading it only during the first pulse.

rewrites.title: Clonal heritability and mitotic bookmarking
rewrites.description: Use expressed lineage barcodes with a split-clone design to test whether re-challenge responsiveness after several divisions is clone-correlated rather than randomly distributed across the population. Pair this with live imaging and single-molecule residence-time measurements of Halo-tagged Fos/Jun during mitosis to test whether AP-1 physically bookmarks target enhancers through cell division.

rewrites.title: 3D genome anchoring of AP-1-primed enhancers
rewrites.description: Use Micro-C or region-capture Hi-C together with AP-1 CUT&RUN before, during, and long after a transient stimulus to ask whether AP-1 establishes persistent enhancer-promoter contacts that outlast the signal. Stable loops anchored at AP-1 sites that remain after factor loss would be a structural substrate for memory, testable by degron removal of AP-1 or by CRISPRi silencing of individual anchors.

rewrites.title: Heritability of AP-1 state through mitosis
rewrites.description: Use a knock-in Fos or Jun live reporter with lineage tracking to sort cells by prior AP-1 history and follow them through several divisions, then test whether daughter cells retain the primed response. Live imaging of chromatin binding during mitosis (mitotic bookmarking) will show whether AP-1 stays bound across division, which would make the memory cell-heritable.

rewrites.title: Mitotic bookmarking by FOS/JUN at memory enhancers
rewrites.description: Test whether AP-1 remains chromatin-bound through mitosis by performing CUT&RUN/CUT&Tag for FOS/JUN and ATAC-seq on mitotically arrested and sorted primed vs. naive cells, paired with live-cell Halo-JUN imaging and FRAP on condensed chromosomes to measure residence time. Then test necessity with a cell-cycle-restricted auxin/dTAG degron that removes AP-1 only during the M-phase window, asking whether daughter cells lose the primed response while cells degraded in G1 retain it.
